vt31_tithe_r.topic: Tithe from voluntary gift to church law and state tax; indulgences, annates, Peter's Pence; church tax today

claims.text: Catholic Encyclopedia: ministers at first supported by 'the spontaneous offerings of the faithful'; earliest positive legislation the letter of the bishops at Tours 567 and canons of Mâcon 585; earliest civil enforcement in Charlemagne's capitularies end of 8th c.; English law recognised tithes under Athelstan, Edgar and Canute, first statute mention Westminster 1285; Lateran III (1179): no alienation of tithes to laymen without papal consent; Saladin tithe under Gregory VIII for those not going on crusade; tithes first payable to the bishop, later to parish priests; Hebrew tithe to Levites, second tithe for feast, triennial tithe for poor

Shuler (Traditio 2012): 'mandatory tithing to the church was not a custom of early Christianity'; first unambiguous developed theory of the tithe from sixth-century Gaul, Caesarius of Arles (c.469-542); 'secular enforcement in 779' a decisive moment

Third Council of Mâcon (585) prescribed excommunication for those who did not pay; Charlemagne divided tithes into four parts (fabric, poor, bishop, parish clergy); England: Tithe Commutation Act 1836 replaced tithes with rentcharges; Tithe Act 1936 converted them to annuities, ended by Finance Act 1977; Germany church tax roughly 8-9% of income tax, basis Art. 140 Basic Law with Art. 137 Weimar Constitution, opt out by written declaration; Catholic Church today no 10% requirement
Capitulary of Herstal, March 779: payment of tithes made obligatory throughout the Frankish kingdom, part for relief of the poor; issued amid famine

August Decrees 1789, art. 5: tithes of every kind abolished, on condition another method be found to pay for worship; tithes collected meanwhile; Sutherland: landlords raised rents by the tithe amount
German Bishops' Conference 2025 statistics: c.19.22 million Catholics (c.23% of population), c.307,000 formal departures in 2025 (321,000 in 2024), Sunday Mass attendance 6.8% (c.1.304 million)
German Catholic dioceses' church tax revenue: €6.751 billion in 2025, €6.628 billion in 2024 (announced 7 July 2026)

2012 German bishops' decree, approved by the Vatican after three years: those who stop paying church tax by leaving barred from sacraments; registered members pay surcharge up to 9% on income tax; Zollitsch quote; We Are Church: works like excommunication

NSS 26 Sept 2012: Federal Administrative Court Leipzig ruled against Hartmut Zapp, who wanted to stop paying church tax but stay Catholic; decree: no sacraments except before death, burial may be refused absent repentance, no church employment, no godparent role; 'one cannot partly leave the Church'

Britannica: first indulgences full remission for crusade and Reconquista; 14th-15th c. complaints of 'sale' by pardoners; secular governments took as much as two-thirds; Tetzel rhyme; Trent 1563 condemned base gain; Pius V abolished the sale of indulgences in 1567; Paul VI reform 1967

Tetzel made indulgence commissioner Jan 1517 for Albrecht; half the money went to Albrecht to pay debts from securing the archbishopric; Pastor: Tetzel's preaching for the dead exceeded official teaching

Albrecht of Brandenburg borrowed 20,000 guilders from Jacob Fugger to pay the confirmation fee to the Curia; proposed indulgence with half to new St Peter's and half to his treasury; bull 31 March 1515; Luther sent the 95 Theses to Albrecht 31 October 1517

Annates: half or all of a benefice's first-year income; Clement V claimed English vacant benefices' first fruits 1305; John XXII all Christendom's for two years 1319; servitia communia; Council of Basel failed to abolish; England: Henry VIII stopped c.1532 (c.£3,000 a year), 1534 Act made them payable to the Crown; Queen Anne's Bounty 1704; France ended 4 August 1789

Peter's Pence: Anglo-Saxon Romefeoh; Ine 725, Offa 794; Canute's 1031 letter: a penny per hearth for households with at least 30 pence rent; ended by Henry VIII's 1534 act; Pius IX's Saepe venerabilis 5 August 1871 formalised lay donations
CIC 222 §1: faithful 'obliged to assist with the needs of the Church' for worship, apostolate, charity and 'the decent support of ministers'

CIC 1260: Church has 'an innate right to require' from the faithful what is necessary; 1261: faithful 'are free to give'; 1263: bishop may impose a moderate tax on juridic persons, extraordinary exaction on others in grave necessity

CCC 2042-2043: precepts: Mass on Sundays and holy days; confession at least once a year; communion at least at Easter; keep holy days; fasting and abstinence; 'duty of providing for the material needs of the Church, each according to his abilities'

vt31_sunday_r.topic: Sunday obligation and church law from Elvira to the Catechism; Gnostic texts on rules

claims.text: Elvira canon 21: 'Si quis in civitate positus tres dominicas ad ecclesiam non accesserit, pauco tempore abstineatur, ut correptus esse videatur' (anyone in a city who stays away three Sundays to be excluded for a short time)

Catholic Encyclopedia 'Sunday': Elvira c.300 canon 21; Constantine's edict barred judges and townspeople from work, agriculture excepted; Apostolic Constitutions (late 4th c.) prescribe Mass and rest; Laodicea: abstain from work on the Lord's day 'as far as possible'; Caesarius of Arles insisted on staying for the whole Mass; Orléans 538 rejected applying Sabbath law to Sunday; from the 8th c. local councils forbade servile work, markets, court pleading
Council of Agde 506: 35 bishops, presided by Caesarius of Arles; canon 7 forbids clergy alienating church property that supports them
Agde 506 required communion of the laity at Christmas, Easter and Pentecost

Lateran IV (1215): every adult to confess to own priest at least once a year and receive the Eucharist at least at Easter, otherwise 'cut off from the Church' in life and 'deprived of Christian burial'; tithes to be paid before taxes, enforced by censure
CIC 1246 §1 Sunday 'the primordial holy day of obligation'; 1247 faithful 'obliged to participate in the Mass' and abstain from work hindering worship

CCC 2181: 'Those who deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin'; 2187 public authorities should ensure time for rest and worship; 2188 Christians 'should seek recognition of Sundays ... as legal holidays'
Gospel of Philip: 'He who has knowledge of the truth is a free man'; 'Ignorance is a slave. Knowledge is freedom.'; 'The law was the tree'
CIC 1983 can. 1364 §1: 'An apostate from the faith, a heretic or a schismatic incurs a latae sententiae excommunication'
Theodosius dealt harshly with Christian apostates (CTh 16.7); Manichaeans deprived of the right to make wills or benefit from them

vt31_economies_r.topic: Comparison of institutional and inner-tradition economies; Cathars; Weber; counter-readings

claims.text: World History Encyclopedia: 'the Cathars all worked, priests as well as laypeople, many as weavers'; Cathar clergy had no possessions; Cathars rejected the Church's acquisition of land and wealth; Council of Saint-Félix 1167 organised bishoprics; men and women could be perfecti
Council of Saint-Félix 1167 (acts printed by Besse 1660 from a lost 1223 copy; authenticity doubted): Bogomil Nicetas consoled Cathar bishops of Toulouse, Albi, Carcassonne, Agen
Credentes not required to live as perfecti; vied to house travelling perfecti; perfecti lived in poverty, abstained from sex and meat; candidates kept vows for life; consolamentum at death

Swatos on Weber: charisma rests on personal relation and is unstable; routinization settles who legitimately holds power (traditional or rational-legal); 'office charisma': a sacred office such as Holy Orders conveys sanctity to its holder's acts regardless of personal character
Metzger (1987) frames: is the canon 'a list of authoritative books, or an authoritative list of books?' and leans to recognition of books already authoritative; canonisation a long gradual process
